summary.text: The Treaty of Versailles was the peace treaty signed on 28 June 1919 that ended the state of war between Germany and most of the Allied Powers.
It required Germany to disarm, make territorial concessions, recognise the independence of states once part of the German Empire, and pay reparations to the Entente powers.
Critics called it both too harsh and too lenient, and bitter resentment of it powered the rise of the Nazi Party and eventually a Second World War.

facts.label: Signed
facts.value: 28 June 1919, at the Palace of Versailles

facts.label: Negotiations
facts.value: Six months of Allied talks at the Paris Peace Conference

facts.value: Not allowed to join the negotiations before signing

facts.label: United States
facts.value: Never ratified it and made a separate peace with Germany

facts.value: The Dawes Plan and Young Plan reduced reparations payments

items.prompt: John Maynard Keynes and Marshal Ferdinand Foch both criticised the treaty. How did their complaints compare?

options.label: Keynes thought it too harsh, while Foch thought it too lenient
Both thought it was far too harsh on Germany
Both thought it was too lenient with Germany
Keynes thought it too lenient, while Foch thought it too harsh

items.explain: Keynes called it a "Carthaginian peace", while Foch criticised it for treating Germany too leniently.

items.prompt: The victors wanted competing, sometimes conflicting things from the peace. How did Germany end up?

options.label: Permanently weakened and fully reconciled
Pacified but permanently crippled
Conciliated but left without any army
Neither pacified nor conciliated, nor permanently weakened

items.explain: The compromise left no one satisfied: Germany was neither pacified nor conciliated, nor permanently weakened.

items.prompt: A country that fought in the war refuses to ratify the main peace treaty. What does it do instead?

options.label: It stays formally at war with Germany for decades
It makes its own peace treaty with Germany, based on the original
It joins Germany to rewrite the treaty's terms
It leaves the peace talks to the League of Nations

items.explain: The United States never ratified the treaty and made a separate peace with Germany, based on the Versailles Treaty.

items.prompt: Fighting ended in November 1918, but the peace treaty came only in June 1919. What filled the gap?

options.label: Fresh fighting that restarted the war
Years of talks with German delegates present
Months of Allied negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference
A wait for the United States to ratify it

items.explain: The armistice ended the actual fighting, but it took six months of Allied negotiations to conclude the peace treaty.

items.prompt: Germany's evacuation of occupied France and Belgium, and its agreed payment for damage, are often blamed on Versailles. Where were they first agreed?

options.label: In the earlier armistice, while the war was still ongoing
In secret talks held after the treaty was signed
In the Fourteen Points issued in January 1918
In the Locarno Treaties that came years later

items.explain: Many aspects later criticised were agreed first in the 11 November armistice agreement, while the war was ongoing.

items.prompt: Bitter resentment of a peace settlement builds in a defeated country. According to this history, what did it help power?

options.label: A return of the Kaiser to the German throne
A lasting alliance between Germany and Britain
The creation of the League of Nations
The rise of the Nazi Party and eventually a second world war

items.explain: Bitter resentment of the treaty powered the rise of the Nazi Party and eventually the outbreak of a Second World War.

paragraphs.heading: The peace that ended a war
paragraphs.text: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919. It was the most important treaty of World War I, bringing the formal state of war to a close between Germany and most Allied Powers. The signing took place in the Palace of Versailles five years to the day after Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated, the event that set off the war. Germany's partners among the Central Powers each signed their own separate treaties.

paragraphs.heading: From armistice to treaty
paragraphs.text: The armistice of 11 November 1918, a deal to stop the fighting, did not by itself make peace. The Allies then negotiated for six months at the Paris Peace Conference before the treaty was ready, and Germany had no part in those talks before it signed. Though the talks are often called the Versailles Conference, only the signing happened at the palace. Most of the bargaining went on in Paris, where the leaders known as the Big Four usually met at the French foreign ministry.

paragraphs.heading: Wilson's Fourteen Points
paragraphs.text: The United States had entered the war in 1917, and President Woodrow Wilson did much to shape the peace terms. On 8 January 1918 he set out the Fourteen Points, a plan built on free trade, open agreements and democracy. It asked for a negotiated end to the war, disarmament across the world, a new Polish state, borders redrawn along ethnic lines, and a League of Nations to protect every state's independence. Germany later sought peace on the basis of these points and said that was the basis on which it surrendered.

paragraphs.heading: What Germany had to do
paragraphs.text: The treaty made Germany disarm and hand over land. It had to give up people accused of war crimes and accept that Kaiser Wilhelm would be put on trial. It had to recognise new independent states carved from territory that had belonged to the German Empire. It also had to pay reparations, which the armistice had described as payment for damage done, to the Entente powers.

paragraphs.heading: Too harsh or too soft
paragraphs.text: Critics such as John Maynard Keynes called the treaty too harsh, a 'Carthaginian peace'. Others on the winning side, such as the French Marshal Ferdinand Foch, said it let Germany off too lightly. Historians and economists still argue the point. The victors' clashing aims produced a compromise that pleased nobody: Germany was not calmed, not won over, and not weakened for good.

paragraphs.heading: What came after
paragraphs.text: The United States never ratified the treaty and instead signed its own peace with Germany, though that deal was based on Versailles. Troubles arising from the treaty led to the Locarno Treaties, which made relations between Germany and the other European powers better. Reparations were reorganised and cut under the Dawes Plan and the Young Plan. Even so, deep resentment of the treaty fed the rise of the Nazi Party and, in the end, a second world war.
